utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Good morning, ladies and gentlemen. Could we have the witness? (Witness entered court)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Please remind the witness he is still under his oath.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Mr. Grubac, may I remind you you are still under oath.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: May we have the appearances, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: If your Honour pleases, my name is Niemann and I appear with my colleagues Ms. McHenry, Mr. Turone and Ms. Van Dusschoten for the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Appearances for the Defence.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Good morning your Honours, my name is Edina Residovic, and I appear for Mr. Zejnil Delalic along with Professor Eugene O'Sullivan, professor from Canada.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: Good morning, your Honours my name is Olujic and I appear on behalf of Mr. Zdravko Mucic, I come from Croatia. My colleague with me in the courtroom is Niko Duric, attorney from Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARABDIC
utterances.text: Good morning, your Honours, I am Salih Karabdic and I appear for Mr. Hazim Delic. With me in the team is Mr. Thomas Moran, attorney from Houston Texas.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Good morning, your Honours, I am John Ackerman and I appear along with my co-counsel Cynthia McMurray on behalf of Mr. Esad Landzo.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Ms. Residovic, I think you are still cross-examining. You may proceed with your cross-examination. Dr. Petko Grubac (continued) Cross-examined by MS. RESIDOVIC (continued)

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Good morning, your Honours, good morning, Mr. Grubac. We discussed yesterday about your testimony in this Trial Chamber. I would now like to ask you some other questions regarding the facts you have testified to, or which I feel you are aware of as an eyewitness of the events. I think that today we also have to bear in mind the warnings of the court in connection with the translation of the questions and answers. Mr. Grubac, in the course of your direct examination you said that while you were working in building 22 at the beginning, that you wrote down in a notebook, as you had used to do in your professional career, some diagnoses of the patients who were in your infirmary. You also said that you did not write down the real diagnosis, but a mild one. Did I understand you well?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I am afraid these earphones are not working properly, so I will not be able hear the translation. If somebody would be kind enough to change these earphones for me, please. (Pause) I can hear you. At the beginning we did record the proper diagnoses, but later on we felt that it might not be a good idea to keep such a record of the actual diagnosis because this could have some adverse effects on us, so we stopped doing it, and eventually we stopped keeping any kind of records.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You also said, Mr. Grubac, that Pero Mrkajic had died in the infirmary. Is it true, as your colleague said, that at the time you said and recorded in the book that he died from diabetes for the reasons that you have now given us?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Did (redacted) say that he put this down or that I had put it down?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: (redacted) said that asked for the cause of death, he said diabetes. My question is, did you put that diagnosis down in the notebook?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not agree at all with (redacted) that Pero Mrkajic died from diabetes. My opinion differs.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Maybe there is a misunderstanding. I know what you said regarding the causes of death of Pero Mrkajic, but because of the circumstances you were in and because of the fear you felt you put down a milder diagnosis. Is it possible that in view of all this you put in the notebook as the cause of death of Pero Mrkajic his diabetes?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: You are saying "put down"? I think that is impersonally -- can I answer whether I wrote down this diagnosis? I think I did not put down that diagnosis, in fact, I think I did not write anything regarding the death of Mrkajic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Since you noted down the milder injuries in the notebook, would it be right to say that without any explanation from you anybody who would look through that notebook would not be aware of all the things that you have been telling us here in this Trial Chamber?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They would not know for two reasons. First, because after a certain period of time we put down milder diagnoses, and the second reason being that after some time we did not record anything in the book.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If I understood you well, in answer to a question from the Prosecution you said that you went to building 6 on several occasions, that sometimes you were escorted by guards and at other times you went on your own when being asked to go there by prisoners. You also said that the treatment Hazim Delic gave you was correct, as well as Pavo Mucic's attitude towards you; whenever you met him he would say hello, ask you how you were and so on. Have I understood and interpreted well this part of your testimony?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, you have, quite well, quite correctly.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is it true, Mr. Grubac, that during your stay in building 22, you were not personally mistreated, physically or in any other way abused? Of course, I know that you were suffering as a man held captive, whose freedom of movement was restricted. My question is: was any kind of force resorted to in treatment towards you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Apart from the fact that I was in a camp, that I was hungry, that I did not have water, that I was living under inhumane conditions, no physical force was used against me, that is true.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: No special stricter or harder sanctions were enforced against you because of something you said or did, apart from what we have already noted?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I did my best not to say or do anything that could provoke the reaction of those people.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. You also said that you were visited by a team of Television Sarajevo, is that true?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It is.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: At the time, you were interviewed by journalists of television Sarajevo, Ms. Jadranka Milosevic and Zvonko Maric; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let us be more precise, you were interviewed by? Jadranka Milosevic and Zvonko Maric was the cameraman?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Possibly, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: As you stated, before talking to you Zvonko Maric filmed the interior of building 22?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, he filmed the interior of building 22.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: After that in front of the entrance to building number 22 you and (redacted) were interviewed by journalist Jadranka Milosevic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If you recall, it was you who were the first to be interviewed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Possibly so.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: After that, (redacted) was the one to answer questions?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Possibly.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When the journalist, Ms. Jadranka Milosevic, was about to terminate the interview, you asked if you could say something in addition to what you had already said in answer to her questions?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not remember that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: After talking to you, Jadranka Milosevic and Zvonko Maric spoke to some of the prisoners, (redacted) and (redacted)?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Those are prisoners who were not in building 22.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, but they were prisoners that you knew were in the prison, and after the interview with you they were also interviewed.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not know, they may have spoken to them before us or after us. I do not know which building they were in. I just know that they were not in building 22.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In that case let me put a direct question to you. Did you watch when, not far from you, in the area in the direction of number 9, the journalists spoke to (redacted) (redacted)?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not recall them being in the vicinity. It is possible, but I really do not recall that. I just know that those men were not in building 22 and I do not remember that they had this interview on the platform in front of the building, but it is possible.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In view of this answer, you cannot testify to the contents of the conversation the journalists had with these prisoners?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I could not.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you tell us when this interview was conducted?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: You heard that when the Prosecution asked me when it happened, my answer was that it is difficult for me to situate in time that interview and visit of the TV team, but I think it was in August after I was released from the camp, but I am not quite sure about it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I would now suggest that we view this TV story. It is Defence exhibit and it is a fragment of a tape that has been admitted into evidence already, but before that, since a man appears in this feature who has asked for protective measures, that we have a closed session while we view this tape so as not to reveal the identity of that witness. Will you please show us segment 2 from exhibit D42. I apologise, I am being told it may be D45, but I think the technical services have the tape with the interview with the journalists, so if I am wrong in citing the number of the exhibit, I apologise, this can be verified. (Closed session)

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: (Open session)

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Dr. Grubac, having seen this story, may I ask you, is that the interview that you granted to the journalists of TV Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, it is and I can now confirm that the interview took place in August after we were released from the Celebici camp, something I could not say with certainty before, and now I can say that on the basis of the clothes I was wearing and the actual text of my statement.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you can confirm that at the end of the interview, when the journalist thought it was over, you wanted to make a clarification and you did so.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Obviously I wanted to say that we, too, were prisoners until only a few days ago and that we had now been released, we were in town and that we come to the camp from town.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And because you were saying that then, you said that you were released three weeks ago, so the interview must have been somewhere in the middle of August or the second half of August?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Grubac, in the course of the examination-in-chief, you said that before this interview you were taken to the command building where you met Mr. Delalic and Mr. Mucic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, after the interview we went to the command building. That is what I said to the Prosecution and that is the truth.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So as you stated here, you met Mr. Delalic in front of the building?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In front of the building and later on in the building after the interview.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you did not see there any other people whom you knew?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not know what you mean when you say other people.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Except for the journalists, Mucic, Delalic, yourself and (redacted) no one else you knew was there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not recall that there were any people that I knew, except for those.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Dr. Grubac, if somebody were to claim that before this interview you were in the command building and that you spoke there with others and that there were other acquaintances of yours in there, then that person would not be telling the truth?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I would not put it that way.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: May I object, please, to this way of putting a question, assuming that other people, without saying whom, is not telling the truth on something. I do not think this is a proper way to ask a question of the witness, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Dr. Grubac, are you sure that you did not go to the command building before the interview and sit there and have a drink there? Are you quite sure of that, that you did not go to the command building before the interview?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not remember going. I will give you the same answer.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If (redacted) were to say that Mr. Delalic's brother was there, then you would say that that is not correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I would not say that, because I cannot tell with absolutely precision who else was there apart from those people that I have named. There may have been some others, but I do not remember, so I would not say that (redacted) was not telling the truth.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let us go back for a moment to the same question in a different way. Mr. Grubac, you were interrogated by the Prosecution on 12th and 13th December 1995; is that so?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: You mean here in the Tribunal?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: No, somewhere else, I do not know where.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Will you please repeat the question for me.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you interviewed in December 1995 by Mr. Ole Hortemo investigator of the OTP?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is it true that you spoke a second time with the investigator of the Tribunal, Ms. Sabine Manke and that you also made a statement on that occasion on 12th November 1996?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you made your first statement, you signed a certificate, a witness acknowledgment, saying that you had made the interview of your own free will, that you were aware that it may be used in legal proceedings before the International Criminal Tribunal, and that you stated everything to the best of your knowledge and recollection; is that so?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Possibly.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is it true, Mr. Grubac, that in that statement you made for the investigator over two days, you did not make any mention of this interview, nor of the presence of Mr. Zejnil Delalic at the interview?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not know, one would have to see the statements and then see whether they contain this or not.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If I were to show you a copy of that statement to refresh your memory, then you would be able to answer that question precisely.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I believe you. If it does not say that in the statement, then I did not say it at the time, but that does not mean to say that this did not happen.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is it true then that you referred to this interview for the first time when questioned by Ms. Sabine Manke on 12th November 1996?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I did not compare my statements, so really I cannot tell you whether this happened for the first time on that particular date or some other, I just cannot tell you that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is it true that you spoke about this incident and you mentioned Mr. Delalic only because you were put a question to that effect explicitly by Ms. Sabine Manke?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not know how Ms. Sabine could have known that Delalic had spoken with me then or not. It is quite possible that I just recalled the incident and told her about it, without knowing how important all that is. I am neither a judge nor an investigator, so I really do not see why this is so important for the court. Maybe on one occasion I did not mention something and I did on another occasion.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you do not exclude the possibility that you spoke about it because the investigator asked you about it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is not what I said.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: My question is: but you do not exclude that possibility?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not wish to answer hypothetical questions, but if you want me to answer them hypothetically, I can, though I think I am a witness and my answers should be very clear.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In the course of my cross-examination yesterday you explained to me your relationship with Mr. Delalic and you told us also that he did not change his attitude towards you even later, and that you addressed him, having a certain amount of trust in him, with the request that he might assist you. I am referring to September, so that you did not feel any fear of Mr. Zejnil Delalic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is not true, that is your assumption. I felt a terrible fear, not only of Zejnil but of the whole situation, and I was afraid of everyone. It would be strange if I had not felt fear in view of all the things that happened to me and it is not true that I thought that his attitude had not changed. That is your interpretation. That is not what I said. I think that everybody's attitude changed, or perhaps this was an attitude they had before and it was I who was wrong, so I could not really tell which is true.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I do not wish to engage in any polemics with you. The transcript has registered your answers to my questions, but let us continue. At the time you were giving this interview, you had already been released from prison?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I can say that only conditionally because the whole of Konjic and the surrounding villages were a great big camp for all Serbs, so you could see that my release papers said that my freedom of movement was limited. You cannot really call that freedom.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said that part of your answers in the interview were not true because you were afraid of the consequences.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is true.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: However, if Mr. Delalic was there, judging by what he had already done for you up to then, you did not expect any consequences to come from Mr. Delalic; is that not so?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, it is not. If you want me to elaborate on this answer, I can.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: No, it is not necessary. If, Mr. Grubac, the journalists Jadranka Milosevic and Zvonko Maric were to say that Mr. Delalic was not there at all, then they would not be telling the truth according to you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They would not be telling the truth and it would not be for the first time. They spoke many untruths on TV Sarajevo. They were well known reporters who told all kinds of stories and that is why I remember their names. Otherwise I would not have remembered them because they are rather insignificant people, but I do remember them precisely because they spoke a lot of untruth and I would not trust them if they were to say that now.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But this interview with you was recorded fully, was it not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I am not even sure of that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well, Mr. Grubac. After this interview, many Serbs criticised you for speaking in quite positive terms about the situation in the camp; is that true?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It is not. I think that the Serbs at that time were unable to see this interview.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Grubac, you certainly are aware of the fact that Mr. Delalic had a lot of problems in Konjic for trying to help you; do you know that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not know how he helped me to have so many problems. Coming from whom?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: From the authorities in Konjic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I thought that he held the highest post in this hierarchy of power in Konjic himself.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You have testified in court that somewhere in mid September you were in the house of Mr. Delalic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And as far as I could understand, that visit was quite friendly, and there was a lot of joking on both sides; is that not so?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: You know how Stalin would assemble his friends in the evening.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I do not know.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I will tell you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: As you described to us yesterday, this was a friendly talk, with joking on both sides, did I hear you well yesterday?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, there was some gallows humour inter alia.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: As you stated yesterday, that was the first time that you learnt that Mr. Delalic was the commander of Tactical Group Number 1?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Is this the full title or is there anything else?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Commander of the First Tactical Group of the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that is true.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And then you also learned that he was spending a lot of time in the vicinity of Sarajevo on Igman where his seat actually was?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: What do you mean? How could I have found out that from this one sentence which he addressed to me which was an offer for me to go to the hospital on Igman? Possibly, but how do you think I could have concluded that on that basis? I did not come to that conclusion, but it is possible.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did Mr. Delalic talk to you about what he was doing as the commander of the tactical group in the theatre near Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He did not introduce himself to me as the commander of this tactical group, so I had no idea that was what he was and I did not know what Mr. Zejnil Delalic was doing exactly at the time. I thought, if you want me to tell, he was considered to be a high officer of the Patriotic League.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: However, you did know that Zejnil Delalic was not on good terms with the chief of MUP, Jasmin Guska, did you not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I did not know that, but it is possible. Before Jasmin Guska, this position was held by a certain Dr. Sejo Hajduk, who was, so to speak, a much more liberal person, and who was not as committed to the SDA as Jasmin Guska was, so he was replaced, and a much more radical person was installed in his stead, which was Jasmin Guska. Sejo was a friend of Zejnil Delalic's, and possibly on that basis, I do not know what other basis could have been there, I do not know that their relationship was not a correct one.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Grubac, in the conversation you had with the representative of the Prosecution in 1995, you as a man who had lived in Konjic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I am sorry, I did not hear the first part of your question.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In your talk about the Prosecutor in December 1995, you as a person who was familiar with the structures and the personages in Konjic, sought to tell or tried to tell the Prosecutor who certain persons were in Konjic at the time. On page 10 of the Serbo-Croat translation of your statement, the following reads, and please be so kind as to confirm whether you indeed said so: "In my opinion, during the conflict in Konjic, the most influential and the most responsible were the following persons: Rusmir Hadzihuseinovic, chairman of the SDA and of the war presidency; Jasmin Guska, chief of the MUP and secretary of the SDA; Esad Ramic, commander of the TO; Dinko Zebic, commander of the HVO, Sefko Niksic, commander of police; Zvonko Zovko, commander of a HVO unit; Midhat Pirkic, commander of a Muslim brigade; Jasna Dzumhur, responsible for the exchange of prisoners and the issuance of various permits; Zejnil Delalic, commander of the tactical group of the BH army." Did you communicate in this way what was written in your statement?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In view of the fact that you were familiar with the circumstances there and these facts, can you confirm that at the time, Ivan Asinovic was the President of the deputy commander of the HVO in Konjic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is correct, if his name is Ivan, I know him as Ivica, but if that is his name, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And that Dr.agan Peric was the President of the HDZ, President of the government or of the executive council of the commune of Konjic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: You mean Dragomir Peric.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Or Drago?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That Omer Boric was for a time the commander of the TO headquarters?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That Nedzo Stojanovic, known as Kiso, earlier the holder of offices in the municipality of Konjic and while you were still there, which is to say towards the end of 1992 and the beginning of 1993, vice-president of the war presidency of the municipality of Konjic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is not true, or I do not know that that is so. Kiso while I was in Konjic was not the vice-president of the war presidency, or at least I was not aware of that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That Dragan Andric was the assistant commander of the staff of the TO of Konjic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Possibly, these are some precise particulars which I could not exactly confirm but it is possible.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know what Zeljko Mlikota was?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Probably the commander of a HVO unit somewhere out there, I am not sure. There were so many armies and so many commanders, it was really hard to tell who belonged to what.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You also stated that in October 1995, the MUP arrested you and your wife again?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, on 4th October they took us to the MUP prison.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you stayed there until 24th December 1992?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Or 25th , yes, that is so.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you were helped then by Goran Blazovic, who used to be a MUP Inspector before that and at that time he was a member of the HVO; is that not so?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He then assumed this position of deputy commander, deputy chief of the MUP. It is possible that before that he had been the commander or the head of MUP, or an inspector, sorry, I am not quite sure. It is possible.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: At that time some guards told you that Jasmin Guska had arrested you because of the possibility of being exchanged for the bodies of the mother and sister of your colleague Sejo Buturovic who had been killed somewhere in the area in the direction of Borci; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That was one of the variants we heard from the guards. I do not know whether they were well informed. No one of the officials talked to us about it, but that is true that we were told that also.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: During your stay in prison you probably learned that Mr. Delalic had left Konjic and gone abroad.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, we learned that he had left Konjic but we did not know to where he had returned at that time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In the prison and after you had left it, you probably heard various rumours which were being bandied about in Konjic at the time, claiming that Zejnil Delalic had fled aboard a Chetnik helicopter and he had gone to the Serb side?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I have not heard this variant, that he had aligned himself with the Serbs. I heard various stories about the actual way in which he had escaped from Konjic. I heard the variant that he had gone across Serb held territory, but not aboard a Chetnik helicopter and I did not know that he was in Serb held territory.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You also heard that he was being criticised for having helped the Serbs and that they were saying that he was a collaborator of the KOS?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not know how he helped the Serbs and I would like to hear one single example of how someone helped the Serbs in Konjic. I would be glad to hear that. I have no knowledge of any such examples. You mean Schindler List or something like that?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I was not in Konjic myself, Mr. Grubac, I cannot discuss the matter with you. I am asking you and please answer to the best of your knowledge.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I believe that no one helped the Serbs at that time. They were all seeking to destroy the Serbs in the municipality of Konjic, and they almost succeeded.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know, Mr. Grubac, that the first aid of the UNHCI only arrived in Konjic in the first half of August?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I am not aware of that, but it is of no consequence because the Serbs were not given any assistance, and all the money and the food they did have was looted from them, so this is an immaterial factor, as far as the Serbs were concerned. I did not get any -- I did not know of it, and if I did know, it would have been to no avail.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If (redacted) were to confirm in court, before this Tribunal, that a large quantity of flour was given to the Serbs in Donje Selo, you are simply unaware of that fact, is that so?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I have my opinion about (redacted). Let the court appraise his statements. It is possible he said this flour was distributed. I could not move, I could not go to Donje Selo. My movement was restricted.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In connection with the persons that we mentioned before, you know that Djuro Kuljanin was the vice president of the assembly of the municipality of Konjic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I do, that is true.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you are aware of the fact that in the second half of April he went to Borci?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I heard that. I could not confirm at what time exactly, I know that he went to Borci.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If (redacted) said that people who sought to help the Serbs, of which there were not many, but there were some, were considered to be fifth columnists and suffered various consequences in an overall atmosphere also on the part of the authorities in Konjic, could you agree to such a statement?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I could not agree with such a statement, but I could say that there were some individuals who did help some individual Serbs, and assistance or help is a relative term. I could not agree that this was on a larger scale or any scale which was significant. I do not know of any consequences of anyone having any consequences because there were no associations nor any larger groups helping the Serbs, apart from honourable individuals.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you believe that Mr. Delalic was among these honourable exceptions?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I would believe that if you were to enumerate ten Serbs or five Serbs whom he had helped. I have not heard that he assisted the Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Grubac, I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Mr. Olujic, your cross-examination. Cross-examined by MR. OLUJIC

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, your Honours. Good morning, Dr. Grubac.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You must be tired after two days of testimony both from the examination-in-chief and the cross-examination, but I hope we will get through this without any major difficulties. Let me tell you straight away that I do not intend to take too long, but I ask you, with regard to the questions I put to you, to bear in mind the technical aspects, so that everybody in the courtroom can follow what we are saying and to avoid the impression that we are conducting a dialogue for our own benefit only. Dr. Grubac, you said in your testimony when questioned by my learned colleague that until the horrors of war you were head of the clinic in Konjic, is that correct, or head of the health centre, rather?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was doctor of one of the departments of the health centre, that is true.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In view of your specialisation and post graduate studies, did you engage in forensic psychiatry as well?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The Ministry of Justice of the former Bosnia-Herzegovina did give to me the title of permanent expert witness attached to the courts of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Which courts did you testify before as an expert, was that in Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Most frequently in the court in Konjic and occasionally in Sarajevo as well.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you provide expert opinions in other courts on the territory of the former state?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think I did not, I cannot recall.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: During the direct examination, you said that you were replaced because of your ethnic background; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It is correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you have any document about it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not even have an ID card or any other document. I am a man without documents, without property and without a permanent residence.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where are you living now, doctor?

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: Objection, your Honour. There is no reason why the witness should say where he lives now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: I do not see the problem. Why are you frightened about where he lives?

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: There might be a general safety reason for which the witness might not be willing to say where he lives now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: You say this question should not be asked; why do you suggest an answer? That is not on.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: I simply objected so the witness should have the opportunity of choosing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Is it because he is a protected witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: No, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: What was your reason for this?

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: It is the general policy of the Prosecution objecting whenever the question to the witness is going to deal with their real address in public.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: The Prosecution adopts a policy without any regard for the rules of the court.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Might I be able to address the court, your Honour, I might be able to assist?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: I do not know how useful your address will be.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: May I address, your Honour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Yes, you may, but I think it is very awkward and impertinent.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Your Honour, throughout the course of the Tadic hearing, this question was raised a number of times and the court ruled on a number of occasions that the current address of the witness was not to be made public and was not to be divulged. This was based on the fact that the court had accepted the situation that existed in the former Yugoslavia and that if counsel were permitted to probe into current addresses, then when these witnesses returned to the former Yugoslavia or to wherever, because the position could apply anywhere in the world, that these people could be subjected to repercussions as a consequence of giving evidence. The Trial Chamber was satisfied by this and had so ordered. Your Honours, this Tribunal has absolutely no power whatsoever to assist anybody in any part of the world after they have given their evidence, no power. It is because of that the only assistance that can be given is assistance to witnesses when they are here and that certain cautions need to be taken while here in order to protect witnesses, because if it cannot happen here, it cannot happen anywhere.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Frankly, I have heard you at length, I am not sure you have any other things to add. You know this court has rules for the protection of witnesses even before they come to give evidence. You know that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: But apart from that, the information can be kept away from the public if the question is important enough. He can ask for a closed session if it is important for him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Let me get at the root of this, I regard as rudeness on the part of a Prosecution policy, a private policy you made for the guidance of your Prosecution you impose on the Trial Chamber without regard to the rules enabling the Trial Chamber to protect witnesses. All witnesses are entitled to protection, and you give reasons why there should be a greater protection other than that which the rules provide. You are now telling the Trial Chamber that every witness which appears before the Trial Chamber is entitled not to disclose his current address if there is a reason for it.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Your Honours, there exists already, I understand, a ruling from this Chamber that the current addresses of the witnesses need not be given in terms of the handing over of their statements. This is merely an extension of that ruling, in my submission.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: For even witnesses who have not sought protection?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Yes, your Honour, and indeed --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Actually those rules are not binding, as far as I am concerned, especially when there is good reason for telling me there is no need to disclose such a residence, and in the first place, as a matter of ordinary judicial ethics, when such questions are asked, the first thing for any counsel is not necessary to object to the question, but to point out that the question might be unfair. Mr. Turone leaps up as if he was being pursued by someone else and behaved as if everything was at stake here. Your witness came before this Trial Chamber without any pretence that he was frightened of anything, and from what he has said, he has no ID card, he has no papers, he has no residence. It was very easy for the Trial Chamber to protect him. He has made it clear that he had no residence, so I did not see any reason why somebody should invoke a protection policy which, as far as I am concerned, does not exist, according to our rules. If you need protection for a witness you have to apply for that protection and give reasons for it. If any witness who comes up to the witness chair, and at that stage invokes the protection, let there be no way of determining whether the protection was deserving or not and if that is what any Trial Chamber has decided, the law is very clear as to the bindingness of the rule of one Trial Chamber against the other.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Your Honours, in addition to those matters, your Honour -- in view of what your Honour has said, we would ask that there be a short adjournment so we can consult the witness on this question alone. No other issue will be raised with the witness and Mr. Turone will not speak to the witness. I will have Ms. McHenry speak to the witness to ascertain whether or not there are security concerns. I then foreshadow, your Honour, that I will file a general motion before the Chamber that current names of addresses of all witnesses that come before the Chamber may not be disclosed unless, of course, special application is made by the Defence in order to demonstrate that for some particular reason on that particular occasion the address is required and then we can deal with it on an individual basis.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: I do not even see the need for the application and I think from the earlier answers given by the witness himself, that question itself is irrelevant. He has no identity, nothing, and he can proceed to any other question which he wanted. If you have any proper reason for making an application, the Trial Chamber will listen to it. Mr. Olujic, carry on with another question.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: Thank you, your Honours. Dr. Grubac, will you please answer my previous question, or do you want me to repeat it?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: No, I have told you, he has given an earlier answer indicating he has no identity or residence. There is no way you can proceed with that question. That is fairly clear.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: Dr. Grubac, in the direct examination you said that Defence had been organised in Bradina, did you not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I said that this could be called defence only conditionally, that it would be more correct to say that these were village -- this was village guard duty, protecting the village, the old people, the women and children from the infiltration of any groups.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How can you organise defence without military equipment?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I am not a military expert, I am a psychiatrist.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let us recall the period in 1995. Is it true that some time in 1995 Mr. Zdravko Mucic called you up on the phone and that you spoke to him on the phone?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It is true that he called me up, it may have been in 1995.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How long did that conversation last?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Very brief, it was a very brief conversation.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What did you discuss?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He called me up, I asked him where he was calling from and why he was calling me. We asked each other what we were doing. He told me that he was in Germany, that he was having some problems, that he had been charged by the Muslims and that he thought that the Serbs would bring charges against him as well. That was more or less the conversation. He also asked about (redacted) and asked for his telephone number -- no, I am sorry, I do not know whether he asked for his telephone number. He just asked about him.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you give him (redacted) telephone number?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I cannot remember.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: As a psychiatrist, doctor, after leaving the camp did you assist your former colleague detainees?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: You mean in Konjic or later on?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Later on.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Are you in touch with them now?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: One might say that I am in touch with some of them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Have you listened to their terrible stories at length?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I know those stories even without them, but I have listened to their stories.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is there some kind of an organised association of former detainees?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, there is, of course.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Are you a member of that association?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I am a member of that association.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Are you assisting them in a professional way?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I have no such position because the association is a non-governmental organisation and it is based some distance away from where I am now living and it is not possible anyway to organise any kind of aid of that kind.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where is the organisation based?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In the direct examination, doctor, you said that you had lived in Konjic. Can you tell us what the share of Serbs in Konjic was in 1991?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: According to the 1991 census, I think 15 or 16 per cent.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And the Croats?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: 27 per cent.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And Muslims?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Muslims, 52 per cent, but that is not all. There were 5 per cent Yugoslavs and 1 per cent others.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is it true what you said, talking to the Prosecution, that you were replaced as a doctor; is that right, because that is what it says, because as far as I know, there is no position of a doctor, you need to have a post, the name of the post.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I intervened and asked this to be corrected. Of course, one cannot be dismissed as a doctor, one can only be dismissed from the post of director and I think this was an error and I think the correction was made.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: During your testimony you said that you were slapped at the beginning of your detention, that is upon your arrest; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, in the MUP building at Musala in Konjic, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And after that you were never physically mistreated, were you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: One might say so, but only relatively speaking.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You also mentioned in your direct examination some baseball bats. Do you know how many baseball clubs there were in Bosnia-Herzegovina in 1992?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I had never heard of baseball being played in Bosnia-Herzegovina at all. I do not even know how you play the game.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know how long and heavy a baseball bat is?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Probably the prisoners in Celebici who suffered and were in touch with Delic's baseball bat could answer that question better than me. I am afraid I cannot give you a precise answer.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In the course of your direct examination you said that Mr. Mucic took prisoners from the 3rd March school out of fear that they should not be hit by enemy shell fire; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He took us from the 3rd March school saying that that was the reason, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know what happened to the school afterwards? Was it hit by a shell, or what happened to it after the attack?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think the school was never hit because later I lived near the school, less than 100 metres away.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I would like to hear your impression regarding Mucic's company; in other words did you feel quite safe in his company? You could not expect him to start beating him out of the blue just like that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Of that, I was indeed quite sure.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In spite of all the differences we have it is most important that we ascertain the truth, so I am asking you, in view of your detention in the Celebici camp, and I can only but try to understand you, of course I cannot fully sympathise because I have never been through it; can it be said that in the Celebici camp there was a proper sort of military order with the necessary hierarchy and chain of command and everything that implies in the camp?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think there was some kind of order and that everything functioned according to pre-agreed rules.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was there any raising of the flag and saluting the flag in the morning in the camp?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In front of the command building where this would normally take place, there was no such salute, as far as I can recall.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was there an evening roll call?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not know, I was a prisoner. I was not an officer there, so I do not know these things.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You described hangar number 22 and who provided the treatment, you and (redacted), among others. Did Dr. Zrinko Brekalo, Dr. Mandic, Dr. Alen, medical technician known as Ante, a medical technician whose surname was Pekic, did they also come to that infirmary?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Not to the infirmary. I think that one of those doctors did come to the command building once. Some technicians did come to remove the plaster from Mrkajic's leg.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did they bring some medical equipment?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, we had no medical equipment.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did they bring some medicines?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Perhaps somebody did bring some medicines, but not in any significant quantity that I could remember, but certainly they did not bring any equipment because we did not have any.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In addition to these people mentioned, did other doctors come, too, like Dr. Stojanovic, medical technician Zivak, medical technician Mihajlo?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I know these people you have mentioned, Dr. Stojanovic, Mihajlo Magazin, they never came to the infirmary while I was there, maybe later.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: I think it is time for the break so perhaps we should have our break now your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: You will continue after the break at 12.00 pm. (11.30 am) (A short break) (12.00 pm)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: You may proceed, Mr. Olujic.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: Thank you, your Honours. Dr. Grubac, you have come to The Hague together with your wife?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I suppose that you are accomodated together?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We are accomodated at the same hotel.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell me, Dr. Grubac, when you were moved from the 3rd March school, was there any shelling of Konjic at that time when you were transferred?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I did not understand your question.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: After you had been transferred from the 3rd March school, was there any shelling of Konjic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not know, I was in Celebici after that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And were there any injured people that you had to treat for wounds inflicted by the shelling?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, they brought two injured people from the sports hall in Musala.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: During the examination-in-chief, you said that in addition to the other injured they were also Mr. Miro Golubovic, Jarko Mrkajic, called Zara; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell me doctor, do you know who they were injured by?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Miro Golubovic or Golub was brought a bit later in relation to the time when we came to the camp, he was in building 22 for a hour or two hours, that was his first visit, then they took him away after ten or fifteen days, they brought him again to number 22 and he told us how he had been tortured and inflicted pain in the camp.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And Zara Mrkajic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We saw him quite often, Zara, he would come from number 9 to take food and to take food back to the prisoners in building number 9.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: During the examination-in-chief you said that you never informed anyone about the health status of the patients, is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you perhaps inform Mr. Mucic about it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He never enquired and we never informed him, he was not interested in the health condition of the patients.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you perhaps inform your Croatian colleagues or the other doctors who came?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No one came to building number 22 to enquire about the health of the patients.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: During the examination-in-chief, you said that until 1990 you had been a member of the League of Communists and after 1990, you became a member of the Movement for Yugoslavia, is that so?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is not so. I will give you a precise answer. From 1990 and in 1991, we tried to form a group of Muslims, Croats and Serbs for this movement, but we did not succeed so we did not register our group nor did we form that movement.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How come you did not succeed to do that in a mixed ethnic community?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: People were more interested in the nationalist ethnically based parties than in this sort of a group or association.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said in your statement that the release papers which you received were signed in your case by Mr. Zejnil Delalic. Do you know of any other releases that took place in August, for instance, two of your brothers-in-law who were also in the camp?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, my brothers-in-law were not released at all, they were transferred to the Musala building in Konjic and after a certain period of time one of them was released and the other one was exchanged to Trnovo.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who signed their release papers?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not know what you mean by theirs, because one of them was not released at all. I do not know whether there are any signatures on the other.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was it Mr. Zdravko Mucic that released the prisoners as far as you know?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I witnessed him releasing Golubovic precisely from building number 22 and taking him away.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I believe he took him home when he released him from the camp. Possibly he took him elsewhere, but he certainly released him from the camp, I can say that with precision.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: During the examination-in-chief, you said that when you were asked what you were by nationality, you said that you were a Serb and a Montenegran, is that so?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How can that be? I fail to perceive how you can be both.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Montenegrans consider that Montenegrans are Serbs. Until recently I was Yugoslav and I found it much easier now to say I am a Serb Montenegran.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: Thank you, doctor, I am through. Thank you, your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Any other cross-examination?

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: May it please the court?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Yes, you may proceed. Cross-examined by MR. MORAN

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, your Honour. Good afternoon, sir.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: My name is Tom Moran and I represent Hazim Delic. I am going to ask you a few questions about some of the things you testified about yesterday and some other things about the camp. If you do not understand one of my questions, will you stop me and ask me to rephrase it or do whatever it takes so you understand what I am asking?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You will do that for me, sir?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I will, sir.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And also if you just listen to the question that I ask and just answer the question that is posed to you, this will go a whole lot easier and a whole lot quicker, and we will get you home, wherever home is, a whole lot quicker. Will you do that for me, doctor?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: By the way, doctor, just so I am straight in my own mind, in my country it is traditional to call physicians by their title doctor and I notice that some of the lawyers from the former Yugoslavia were calling you Mr. Which is correct and which do you prefer?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It is all the same to me. Many things do not make much of a difference to me any more.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I can understand that doctor. You worked probably a lot harder for your doctor's degree than I did for mine, so why don't I call you doctor? Would that be fair?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The first thing I am going to ask you, and this goes back to your initial arrest and your initial detention, you were taken to the MUP headquarters in Konjic; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And it was at the MUP headquarters at Konjic where all your property was taken from you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: As far as you know, there was not anybody from the camp at Celebici that was there involved in the taking of your property, was there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you very much on that, doctor. I wanted to make sure I was clear in my mind on that. I would like to talk to you now a little bit about the conditions in the infirmary in building 22 while you were there, and some of the things I think you may have already talked about and we will go over those in a little bit of detail and some of the other things I do not think anybody has talked about. Let us start off with, like I say, some of the general living conditions there. Let us start off with the food that was served to the patients in building 22 and how it was served. Everybody in building 22 had their own plate and fork, did they not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: No? How was the food served to the patients in building 22?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We would bring the food in a soldier's pot.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were there plates for the individual patients to eat from?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, not all the patients had a plate. In fact we had no plates at all, but we had these vessels of army issue, containers, not one to each patient. We all had five or six of them and we all used these five or six; that is to say not every patient had one of those containers for himself.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were there not a couple of great big large plates of some kind that you used to serve bread on?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, there were no plates of that kind.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Let us talk about some of the other conditions. How about showers? Showers were available for the patients in the infirmary, were they not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So the patients were not taken to one of the other buildings and given a chance to shower and use the toilet?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, we used the toilet in the other building, in the command building, and during my stay over a period of two months we only had a chance to take one shower, only on one occasion and that, of course, only referred to the patients who were mobile and the two of us doctors.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let me go on to something else. Let us talk about the death of Pero Mrkajic, okay? You testified, I believe, on direct examination that at the time of his death, Mr. Delic brought his family in to let them see the body and to say goodbye to their relative; do you recall testifying to that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, he brought not the whole family but two of his sons who were also imprisoned in the camp, Jarko Mrkajic and Desimir Mrkajic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: He did more than that, did he not? For instance, he got some candles, do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I really do not recall that. It is possible.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Let me jump a little bit ahead and I think we may jump back to something also, but while I am thinking about it. After your release from Celebici Mr. Delic took you to your former apartment, did he not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I apologise, will you please repeat the question?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sure. After you were released someone else was living in the apartment in Konjic that used to be your apartment, were they not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, they were.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But all of your property was still in your apartment, all your furniture and your clothing and all of those things will be left there, right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did not Mr. Delic after your release take you to your apartment so that you could retrieve some of your property, whatever you wanted?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, just to get some things.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you recall whether or not the person that was living in that apartment refused Mr. Delic entry?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And that Mr. Delic essentially forced his way in so that you could recover what of your property you wanted to recover?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is true.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you were living at your father-in-law's apartment Mr. Delic brought you some flour and oil and detergents and shampoo, and things like that, did he not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, my father-in-law, yes, and he did bring me a package with food, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: While he was there you mentioned to him that your children were sick and needed some medication, did you not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It is possible, but I really do not remember.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Perhaps do you recall writing a prescription for some medicine at your father-in-law's house and having Mr. Delic go to the -- go some place to get the medication that you requested?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is possible and I believe he would have done it, but I really cannot recall that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In fact, Mr. Delic was the source of most of the medication that you had in the infirmary while you were there; is that not right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I am about set to mention a name, and it is the name of a protected witness that has been mentioned in open court. Do you want to go into private session so I can tell this person what the name is, and use the acronym? How do you want me to proceed, your Honour? Whatever you want.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: We will maintain the protection if it is a protected witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Your Honour then perchance we should go into private session so I can identify this person. It will be 30 seconds. (In closed session)

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: (In open session)

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: In fact, you got some medicines from what, Caritas, did you not, catholic charities?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Possibly, I do not know from whence the medicaments came, possibly.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If Witness P said that, you would not disagree with him, would you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I would agree, I would not deny it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You and the other medical people in the infirmary to get medicines on a regular basis would give a list to Mr. Delic, and then he would go wherever he went to try and get the medicines for you, right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, in the beginning that was the way it was, right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You testified, and frankly Witness P testified also, that a lot of the time you did not get everything you asked for, but one of the things that Witness P said, that most of the things you got were analgesics and antibiotics and because there were a lot of elderly people, you got diuretics. Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that is true.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Doctor, are you familiar with the availability of medicines and medical equipment in the Konjic area generally, in the summer of 1992?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I would separate the medicaments and medical supplies. I am not quite sure what you mean by medical equipment -- I mean by medical equipment apparatus as in such things -- perhaps you mean also bandages. I would like to separate these two.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: By equipment I mean things that are more permanent things, everything from your stethoscope to a CAT scan machine, things that you do not use up.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We had no intention and we knew that we would not be able to get such instruments and such equipment. What could be done is for our patients to be taken to a hospital or to a medical establishment and there use such equipment, but that was not done, and we never expected anybody to install a scanner or a X-ray machine in Celebici, but we did expect it would be possible for our patients to go to the health centre in the city and have such examinations performed there, but it did not happen.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Doctor, what I was asking you about was the availability of these kinds of things, and whether you are familiar with the availability of medical supplies, medicines, bandages, consumable items and of permanent equipment in the Konjic area in the summer of 1992, and if you are not familiar with it, that is just fine. If you do not know, you do not know.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I am quite familiar with the situation, I was the manager of this establishment for a while. I know how equipped it was. I know full well what equipment they had. It is quite possible that at the time there was a shortage of some medicaments or of some other material.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know how the demands on the hospital in Konjic at the time you were there, whether it was full of sick people and wounded people much more than it was designed for, or whether the patient load was within what would be considered normal? If you do, you do, if you do not, you do not. If you are not familiar with it, that is fine.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think that that could not have been the reason for these injured people not to be given the same medicaments and the same material which they needed, like those people who were treated in the health centre. I think they were discriminated against in that respect and that the reason was not the shortage but the absence of a will to do so.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That is fine. The question I asked was, are you familiar with the situation. Are you familiar with the situation? Remember, you were in the camp, you may not know what was going on there.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Although they had told us they would treat us according to the Geneva Convention, we were in no position to communicate with the doctors and other staff in the health centre, so that we had no way to come by such information. We did not go there for medicaments. We did not consult with the physicians there because we were not permitted to do so, so we did not know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let us talk about this ledger or log book you kept for medical records. I know you do not have access to it any more, and in fact, at some point within a few weeks after you were released you stopped going to Celebici and started go to another facility, the sports hall, is that not right, so you would have lost track of what occurred with this ledger?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If Witness P says that one of the reasons that that book is not available is that the people in the infirmary were given rations of tobacco but no cigarette paper and used that ledger for cigarette rolling paper, you would not disagree with that, would you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I would not, although I would not exactly advocate the truthfulness of that claim.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If you would like I will read it directly from the transcript to you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not doubt that he said so, and I say I would not deny it, but I would not exactly subscribe to that claim myself.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Simo Jovanovic; he was one of the injured people in the camp, is that not right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I am sorry, I did not hear you well.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Simo Jovanovic; he was one of the injured people in the camp that you treated.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Treated conditionally speaking, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: He had been held by the MUP for three weeks in Konjic, had he not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, he had.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: While he was there he was beaten and mistreated by a man named Jasmin Guska; is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is what I was told.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That is what you believe to be correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I have no reason not to believe it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Fair enough, doctor. A couple of other things and then I think we will be done. I am not trying to jump around, but I am going to jump around a little bit. I am not trying to confuse you. Let us talk about the village of Bradina for just a couple of seconds. In Bradina, that was a major communications link between Sarajevo and the rest of Bosnia-Herzegovina, was it not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Bradina had nothing to do with the blockade of Sarajevo, which was at the time under total blockade. But theoretically, yes, Bradina is along the main communication between Sarajevo and Mostar, but Sarajevo at the time was under blockade for other reasons. Bradina was not of any major significance at the time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The main road between Sarajevo and Mostar and the main railroad go right through the middle of Bradina, do they not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The railroad going from Pluzine to Sarajevo does pass through Bradina, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The residents of Bradina, for whatever reason, set up roadblocks inside the city to control who went through the village on that main road, did they not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, along the main road, but not the railroad, correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Those people that set up those roadblocks were not officials or authorised to do that by the government of Bosnia-Herzegovina, were they?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
